13. Basics of Machine Learning

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Machine learning seeks useful structure in data and predictors that remain accurate on new observations. We begin with dimensionality reduction and clustering, then develop regression and classification through empirical risk minimization, regularization, and kernel methods. Connections with inverse problems explain the role of model assumptions, while the final analysis of generalization balances approximation error against the statistical complexity of the chosen model class.

Imaging problems often concern the reconstruction or processing of an individual signal or image, whereas machine learning studies patterns across collections of observations. Their goals and performance measures differ, but both use tools such as linear models, regularization, and convex optimization.

13.1 Unsupervised Learning¶

In unsupervised learning, we observe nnn points (xi)i=1n(x_i)_{i=1}^n(xi​)i=1n​.

The aim is to identify structure in these observations, for example to visualize them or group them into clusters.

We assume for simplicity that the observations lie in Euclidean space, xi∈Rpx_i \in \mathbb{R}^pxi​∈Rp, where ppp is the number of features. We store the observations as the rows of a matrix X∈Rn×pX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}X∈Rn×p.

13.1.1 Dimensionality Reduction and PCA¶

Dimensionality reduction produces a compact representation of the data for visualization or subsequent analysis. By retaining informative features, it can also reduce computational cost and improve prediction.

Principal component analysis (PCA) projects the data orthogonally onto the principal axes of the covariance matrix.

13.1.2 Clustering and kkk-means¶

Clustering assigns a label yi∈{1,…,k}y_i \in \{1,\ldots,k\}yi​∈{1,…,k} to each observation xix_ixi​. Observations with the same label form a cluster.

kkk-means

One approach is to seek compact clusters by minimizing a measure of within-cluster dispersion. In Euclidean space, the kkk-means objective measures distances from observations to their centroids c=(cℓ)ℓ=1kc=(c_\ell)_{\ell=1}^kc=(cℓ​)ℓ=1k​, with cℓ∈Rpc_\ell \in \mathbb{R}^pcℓ​∈Rp. Related formulations are possible in general metric spaces, although the centroid computations may be more difficult. The optimization problem is

min⁡(y,c)  E(y,c):=∑ℓ=1k∑i:yi=ℓ∣ ⁣∣xi−cℓ∣ ⁣∣2.\underset{ (y,c) }{\min}\; \mathcal{E}( y, c ) \mathrel{:=}\sum_{\ell=1}^k \sum_{ i : y_i=\ell } |\!| x_i-c_\ell |\!|^2.(y,c)min​E(y,c):=ℓ=1∑k​i:yi​=ℓ∑​∣∣xi​−cℓ​∣∣2.

Figure 13.7. kkk-means clusters according to Voronoi cells.

The kkk-means algorithm alternates between updating the labels and updating the centroids, a form of block coordinate minimization.

Initialize the centroids ccc, for example by choosing well-separated observations. We discuss a more systematic initialization below.

For fixed centroids ccc, minimize y↦E(y,c)y \mapsto \mathcal{E}(y,c)y↦E(y,c) by assigning each observation to its nearest centroid:

∀ i∈{1,…,n},yi←argmin1⩽ℓ⩽k  ∣ ⁣∣xi−cℓ∣ ⁣∣.(13.7)\forall \,i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}, \quad y_i \leftarrow \underset{1 \leqslant\ell \leqslant k}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; |\!| x_i-c_\ell |\!|. \tag{13.7}∀i∈{1,…,n},yi​←1⩽ℓ⩽kargmin​∣∣xi​−cℓ​∣∣.(13.7)

For fixed labels yyy, minimize c↦E(y,c)c \mapsto \mathcal{E}(y,c)c↦E(y,c) by setting each centroid to the mean of its cluster:

∀ ℓ∈{1,…,k},cℓ←∑i:yi=ℓxi∣{i  ;  yi=ℓ}∣(13.8)\forall \,\ell \in \{1,\ldots,k\}, \quad c_\ell \leftarrow \frac{ \sum_{i : y_i=\ell} x_i }{ | \left\{ i \;;\; y_i=\ell \right\} | } \tag{13.8}∀ℓ∈{1,…,k},cℓ​←∣{i;yi​=ℓ}∣∑i:yi​=ℓ​xi​​(13.8)

If a cluster becomes empty, its centroid does not contribute to the objective for the current labels. One may leave it in place or reseed it at a data point before the next assignment step. The centroid formula applies only to nonempty clusters.

Each step decreases or preserves E\mathcal{E}E. With a fixed tie-breaking rule that retains existing assignments at ties, and without indefinite reseeding, a changed assignment strictly decreases the objective. There are finitely many label assignments, so the algorithm terminates after finitely many such changes.

Because the objective is nonconvex, kkk-means need not find globally optimal clusters.

A reseeding heuristic moves centroids cℓc_\ellcℓ​ from redundant or low-contribution clusters to regions with high distortion. This can help the iterations escape a poor local configuration.

Figure 13.8 shows an example of kkk-means iterations on the Iris dataset.

Figure 13.8. Left: iterations of the kkk-means algorithm. Right: class histograms after the kkk-means optimization.

kkk-means++

The result of kkk-means depends strongly on initialization. Well-separated initial centers tend to cover the data more effectively than tightly grouped centers.

The randomized kkk-means++ initialization has an approximation guarantee even before Lloyd iterations are applied. In practice, Lloyd iterations usually improve the resulting centers. First choose c1c_1c1​ uniformly among the sample points. After choosing c1,…,cℓc_1,\ldots,c_\ellc1​,…,cℓ​, select cℓ+1c_{\ell+1}cℓ+1​ from the sample according to a probability π(ℓ)\pi^{(\ell)}π(ℓ) on {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}{1,…,n} proportional to the squared distance from the nearest selected center

∀ i∈{1,…,n},πi(ℓ):=di2∑j=1ndj2wheredi:=min⁡1⩽r⩽ℓ∣ ⁣∣xi−cr∣ ⁣∣.\forall \,i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}, \quad \pi^{(\ell)}_i \mathrel{:=}\frac{d_i^2}{\sum_{j=1}^n d_j^2} \quad \text{where} \quad d_i\mathrel{:=}\min_{1\leqslant r\leqslant\ell}|\!| x_i-c_r |\!|.∀i∈{1,…,n},πi(ℓ)​:=∑j=1n​dj2​di2​​wheredi​:=1⩽r⩽ℓmin​∣∣xi​−cr​∣∣.

Points far from the previously seeded centers are more likely to be chosen. If every di=0d_i=0di​=0, the current centers already achieve zero distortion and the procedure can stop.

The following theorem, due to David Arthur and Sergei Vassilvitskii, bounds the expected seeding cost by a logarithmic factor times the optimal cost. Computing a global optimum is NP-hard in general.

Theorem 13.5

Let c⋆c^\starc⋆ be the centroids selected by kkk-means++ and let y⋆y^\stary⋆ be their nearest-centroid labels, as in (13.7). Then

E(E(y⋆,c⋆))⩽8(2+log⁡(k))min⁡(y,c)  E(y,c),\mathbb{E}(\mathcal{E}(y^\star,c^\star)) \leqslant 8 (2+\log(k)) \underset{(y,c)}{\min}\;\mathcal{E}(y,c),E(E(y⋆,c⋆))⩽8(2+log(k))(y,c)min​E(y,c),

where the expectation is over the random choices made during initialization.

Lloyd algorithm and continuous densities.

The kkk-means iterations are also known as Lloyd’s algorithm and are used in vector quantization for compression. The same alternating procedure applies to a probability measure μ\muμ on Rp\mathbb{R}^pRp with finite second moment.

The energy to minimize becomes

min⁡(V,c)  ∑ℓ=1k∫Vℓ∣ ⁣∣x−cℓ∣ ⁣∣2dμ(x)\underset{ (\mathcal{V},c) }{\min}\; \sum_{\ell=1}^k \int_{\mathcal{V}_\ell} |\!| x-c_\ell |\!|^2 \mathrm{d}\mu(x)(V,c)min​ℓ=1∑k​∫Vℓ​​∣∣x−cℓ​∣∣2dμ(x)

where (Vℓ)ℓ(\mathcal{V}_\ell)_\ell(Vℓ​)ℓ​ is a partition of the domain.

Step (13.7) is replaced by the computation of a Voronoi cell

∀ ℓ∈{1,…,k},Vℓ:={x  ;  ∀ ℓ′≠ℓ,∣ ⁣∣x−cℓ∣ ⁣∣⩽∣ ⁣∣x−cℓ′∣ ⁣∣}.\forall \,\ell \in \{1,\ldots,k\}, \quad \mathcal{V}_\ell \mathrel{:=} \left\{ x \;;\; \forall \,\ell' \neq \ell, |\!| x-c_\ell |\!| \leqslant|\!| x-c_{\ell'} |\!| \right\} .∀ℓ∈{1,…,k},Vℓ​:={x;∀ℓ′=ℓ,∣∣x−cℓ​∣∣⩽∣∣x−cℓ′​∣∣}.

For distinct centroids, the Voronoi cells are polyhedra bounded by perpendicular bisectors. Resolve distance ties consistently to obtain a partition; this matters if μ\muμ assigns positive mass to a boundary. In low dimensions, computational geometry provides efficient algorithms for constructing the cells.

Step (13.8) is then replaced by

∀ ℓ∈{1,…,k},cℓ←∫Vℓxdμ(x)∫Vℓdμ(x).\forall \,\ell \in \{1,\ldots,k\}, \quad c_\ell \leftarrow \frac{ \int_{\mathcal{V}_\ell} x \mathrm{d}\mu(x) }{ \int_{\mathcal{V}_\ell} \mathrm{d}\mu(x) }.∀ℓ∈{1,…,k},cℓ​←∫Vℓ​​dμ(x)∫Vℓ​​xdμ(x)​.

The centroid update applies to cells of positive μ\muμ-mass; zero-mass cells require a separate convention, as in the discrete algorithm. For a uniform planar density, hexagonal Voronoi patterns are characteristic of high-resolution quantization away from the boundary. They need not be exact finite-kkk minimizers on a bounded domain.

13.2 Empirical Risk Minimization¶

We first describe empirical risk minimization, a framework shared by regression and classification. For classification, predictions may represent class probabilities rather than labels.

To make fitting yi≈f(xi)y_i \approx f(x_i)yi​≈f(xi​) computationally tractable and obtain useful predictions, we restrict the admissible functions to a class of controlled complexity. The class may become richer as the sample size nnn grows, but its complexity must remain compatible with the available data.

13.2.1 Empirical Risk¶

Let Fn\mathcal{F}_nFn​ be a class of functions that may depend on the sample size. A common learning procedure is empirical risk minimization (ERM)

f^∈argminf∈Fn  1n∑i=1nL(f(xi),yi).(13.9)\hat f \in \underset{f \in \mathcal{F}_n}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n L(f(x_i),y_i). \tag{13.9}f^​∈f∈Fn​argmin​n1​i=1∑n​L(f(xi​),yi​).(13.9)

The loss function L:Y2→R+L: \mathcal{Y}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+L:Y2→R+ measures prediction error for the chosen task. Classification and regression typically require different loss functions.

We sometimes write f^n\hat f_nf^​n​ to emphasize the estimator’s dependence on the sample size nnn.

13.2.2 Prediction and Consistency¶

For the analysis, assume the training pairs (xi,yi)(x_i,y_i)(xi​,yi​) are i.i.d. with distribution π\piπ on X×Y\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}X×Y. The corresponding population optimization problem is

fˉ∈argminf∈F∞  ∫X×YL(f(x),y)dπ(x,y)=E(x,y)∼π(L(f(x),y)).(13.10)\bar f \in \underset{f \in \mathcal{F}_\infty}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \int_{\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}} L(f(x),y) \mathrm{d}\pi(x,y) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\pi}\bigl(L(f(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y})\bigr). \tag{13.10}fˉ​∈f∈F∞​argmin​∫X×Y​L(f(x),y)dπ(x,y)=E(x,y)∼π​(L(f(x),y)).(13.10)

The desired consistency property is f^n→fˉ\hat f_n \rightarrow \bar ff^​n​→fˉ​ as n→+∞n \rightarrow +\inftyn→+∞. One way to express this is through expected prediction error over the training samples (xi,yi)i(x_i,y_i)_i(xi​,yi​)i​:

En:=E(L~(f^n(x),fˉ(x)))⟶0.E_n \mathrel{:=}\mathbb{E}( \tilde L(\hat f_n(\mathbf{x}),\bar f(\mathbf{x})) ) \longrightarrow 0.En​:=E(L~(f^​n​(x),fˉ​(x)))⟶0.

Here the expectation includes both the test input x\mathbf{x}x, drawn from the marginal πX\pi_\mathcal{X}πX​, and the nnn i.i.d. training pairs (xi,yi)∼π(x_i,y_i)\sim\pi(xi​,yi​)∼π that determine f^n\hat f_nf^​n​.

The comparison loss L~\tilde LL~ measures discrepancies between predictions in Y\mathcal{Y}Y; for example, we may take L~=L\tilde L=LL~=L. One can also study convergence in probability, i.e.

∀ ε>0,Eε,n:=P(L~(f^n(x),fˉ(x))>ε)→0.\forall \,\varepsilon>0, \quad E_{\varepsilon,n} \mathrel{:=}\mathbb{P}( \tilde L(\hat f_n(\mathbf{x}),\bar f(\mathbf{x})) > \varepsilon) \rightarrow 0.∀ε>0,Eε,n​:=P(L~(f^​n​(x),fˉ​(x))>ε)→0.

These properties define consistency in expectation and in probability, respectively.

A convergence rate gives an explicit upper bound on the decay of EnE_nEn​ or Eε,nE_{\varepsilon,n}Eε,n​.

For L~(y,y′)=∣y−y′∣r\tilde L(y,y')=|y-y'|^rL~(y,y′)=∣y−y′∣r, convergence in expectation implies convergence in probability by Markov’s inequality:

Eε,n=P(∣f^n(x)−fˉ(x)∣r>ε)⩽1εE(∣f^n(x)−fˉ(x)∣r)=Enε.E_{\varepsilon,n} = \mathbb{P}( |\hat f_n(\mathbf{x})-\bar f(\mathbf{x})|^r > \varepsilon) \leqslant\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \mathbb{E}( |\hat f_n(\mathbf{x})-\bar f(\mathbf{x})|^r ) = \frac{E_n}{\varepsilon}.Eε,n​=P(∣f^​n​(x)−fˉ​(x)∣r>ε)⩽ε1​E(∣f^​n​(x)−fˉ​(x)∣r)=εEn​​.

13.2.3 Parametric Approaches and Regularization¶

Instead of specifying Fn\mathcal{F}_nFn​ through a hard constraint, we can favor simple or regular functions through a penalty.

A typical way to achieve this is by using a parametric model y≈f(x,β)y \approx f(x,\beta)y≈f(x,β) where β∈B\beta\in \mathcal{B}β∈B parametrizes the function f(⋅,β):X→Yf(\cdot,\beta) : \mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{Y}f(⋅,β):X→Y. The empirical risk minimization procedure (13.9) now becomes

β^∈argminβ∈B  1n∑i=1nL(f(xi,β),yi)+λnJ(β).(13.11)\hat \beta\in \underset{\beta\in \mathcal{B}}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n L(f(x_i,\beta),y_i) + \lambda_n J(\beta). \tag{13.11}β^​∈β∈Bargmin​n1​i=1∑n​L(f(xi​,β),yi​)+λn​J(β).(13.11)

where JJJ is a regularizer. For example, J=∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣22J=|\!| \cdot |\!|_2^2J=∣∣⋅∣∣22​ controls parameter magnitude, while J=∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣1J=|\!| \cdot |\!|_1J=∣∣⋅∣∣1​ promotes sparse coefficients and, in a linear feature model, feature selection. Here λn>0\lambda_n>0λn​>0 is a regularization parameter, and its asymptotic scaling must balance approximation and estimation; consistency often requires λn→0\lambda_n\to0λn​→0 at a controlled rate.

The population counterpart of (13.10) defines the parameter βˉ\bar \betaβˉ​. A limiting estimator as n→+∞n \rightarrow +\inftyn→+∞ then takes the form fˉ=f(⋅,βˉ)\bar f = f(\cdot,\bar \beta)fˉ​=f(⋅,βˉ​), with βˉ\bar \betaβˉ​ satisfying

βˉ∈argminβ  ∫X×YL(f(x,β),y)dπ(x,y)=E(x,y)∼π(L(f(x,β),y)).(13.12)\bar \beta\in \underset{\beta}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \int_{\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}} L(f(x,\beta),y) \mathrm{d}\pi(x,y) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\pi}\bigl(L(f(\mathbf{x},\beta),\mathbf{y})\bigr). \tag{13.12}βˉ​∈βargmin​∫X×Y​L(f(x,β),y)dπ(x,y)=E(x,y)∼π​(L(f(x,β),y)).(13.12)

Prediction vs. estimation risks.

We may also ask how accurately β^\hat\betaβ^​ estimates βˉ\bar\betaβˉ​, as measured by the parameter error ∣ ⁣∣β^−βˉ∣ ⁣∣|\!| \hat\beta-\bar\beta |\!|∣∣β^​−βˉ​∣∣ for a chosen norm ∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣|\!| \cdot |\!|∣∣⋅∣∣. Parameter estimation is generally more demanding than prediction: different parameters can produce similar predictions, especially when the model is poorly identified.

13.2.4 Validation, Test Sets, and Cross-validation¶

The errors EnE_nEn​ and Eε,nE_{\varepsilon,n}Eε,n​ cannot be evaluated directly because the population optimum fˉ\bar ffˉ​ is unknown.

To tune a parameter such as the regularization strength λ\lambdaλ, we estimate the prediction risk E(L(f^(x),y))\mathbb{E}(L(\hat f(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y}))E(L(f^​(x),y)) on data held out from training.

Use a second sample (xˉj,yˉj)j=1nˉ(\bar x_j,\bar y_j)_{j=1}^{\bar n}(xˉj​,yˉ​j​)j=1nˉ​, called a validation set. In the statistical model, these observations are i.i.d. with distribution π\piπ and independent of the training sample. The validation risk is

Rnˉ=1nˉ∑j=1nˉL(f^(xˉj),yˉj)(13.13)R_{\bar n} = \frac{1}{\bar n} \sum_{j=1}^{\bar n} L(\hat f(\bar x_j),\bar y_j) \tag{13.13}Rnˉ​=nˉ1​j=1∑nˉ​L(f^​(xˉj​),yˉ​j​)(13.13)

which converges to E(L(f^(x),y))\mathbb{E}(L(\hat f(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y}))E(L(f^​(x),y)) for large nˉ\bar nnˉ.

Minimizing RnˉR_{\bar n}Rnˉ​ over hyperparameters (such as λn\lambda_nλn​) is holdout validation. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across folds. A separate test set, untouched by hyperparameter selection, estimates the performance of the final selected procedure.

13.3 Supervised Learning: Regression¶

Figure 13.10. Probabilistic modeling.

In supervised learning, the training data consist of pairs (xi,yi)∈X×Y(x_i,y_i)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}(xi​,yi​)∈X×Y, with X=Rp\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^pX=Rp here for simplicity. We seek a function f:X→Yf:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}f:X→Y that captures the relationship yi≈f(xi)y_i\approx f(x_i)yi​≈f(xi​) and predicts an output f(x)f(x)f(x) for a new input xxx.

When Y\mathcal{Y}Y is finite and discrete, the task is supervised classification, studied in Section 13.4. Binary classification uses Y={0,1}\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1\}Y={0,1}; for example, in a medical application, yi=0y_i=0yi​=0 may indicate a healthy subject and yi=1y_i=1yi​=1 a subject with the condition of interest.

When Y\mathcal{Y}Y is continuous, typically Y=R\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}Y=R, the task is regression.

13.3.1 Linear Regression¶

For regression, we specialize empirical risk minimization to Y=R\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}Y=R with the quadratic loss L(y,y′)=12∣y−y′∣2L(y,y')=\frac{1}{2}|y-y'|^2L(y,y′)=21​∣y−y′∣2.

Nonlinear regression can be formulated using a dictionary of features, such as polynomials. This lifts the data into a higher-dimensional space and leads to the kernel methods of Section 13.5.

Least squares and conditional expectation.

If fff ranges over measurable functions and E(y2)<∞\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{y}^2)<\inftyE(y2)<∞, a population minimizer fˉ\bar ffˉ​ in (13.10) is the conditional mean of the response given the input. It is defined up to equality almost everywhere under the input distribution.

Suppose for simplicity that π\piπ has density dπdxdy\frac{\mathrm{d}\pi}{\mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y}dxdydπ​ with respect to a product measure dxdy\mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}ydxdy, such as Lebesgue measure. Then

∀ x∈X,fˉ(x)=E(y∣x=x)=∫Yydπdxdy(x,y)dy∫Ydπdxdy(x,y)dy\forall \,x \in \mathcal{X}, \quad \bar f(x) = \mathbb{E}( \mathbf{y}| \mathbf{x}=x) = \frac{ \int_{\mathcal{Y}} y \frac{\mathrm{d}\pi}{\mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y}(x,y) \mathrm{d}y }{ \int_{\mathcal{Y}} \frac{\mathrm{d}\pi}{\mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y}(x,y) \mathrm{d}y }∀x∈X,fˉ​(x)=E(y∣x=x)=∫Y​dxdydπ​(x,y)dy∫Y​ydxdydπ​(x,y)dy​

where (x,y)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})(x,y) has law π\piπ and the formula applies where the denominator is positive.

Figure 13.11. Conditional expectation.

If X\mathcal{X}X and Y\mathcal{Y}Y are discrete, let πx,y\pi_{x,y}πx,y​ denote the probability of (x=x,y=y)(\mathbf{x}=x,\mathbf{y}=y)(x=x,y=y). Then

∀ x∈X,fˉ(x)=∑yyπx,y∑yπx,y\forall \,x \in \mathcal{X}, \quad \bar f(x) = \frac{ \sum_{y} y \pi_{x,y} }{ \sum_{y} \pi_{x,y} }∀x∈X,fˉ​(x)=∑y​πx,y​∑y​yπx,y​​

with no prescribed value when the marginal of π\piπ on X\mathcal{X}X vanishes at xxx.

Replacing π\piπ by the empirical distribution averages responses at each observed input but leaves predictions unspecified elsewhere. Generalization therefore requires assumptions on regularity or model complexity.

Penalized linear models.

Figure 13.12. Linear regression.

A linear model constrains fff to have the form f(x,β)=⟨x, β⟩f(x,\beta)=\langle x,\,\beta\ranglef(x,β)=⟨x,β⟩ with parameters β∈B=Rp\beta\in \mathcal{B}=\mathbb{R}^pβ∈B=Rp. Affine predictors are included through the identity ⟨x, β⟩+β0=⟨(x,1), (β,β0)⟩\langle x,\,\beta\rangle+\beta_0=\langle (x,1),\,(\beta,\beta_0)\rangle⟨x,β⟩+β0​=⟨(x,1),(β,β0​)⟩, by appending a constant coordinate to xxx to form (x,1)(x,1)(x,1). We therefore use the linear notation below.

Under the square loss, the regularized ERM (13.11) is conveniently rewritten as

β^∈argminβ∈B  12⟨C^β, β⟩−⟨u^, β⟩+λnJ(β)(13.14)\hat \beta\in \underset{\beta\in \mathcal{B}}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \frac{1}{2} \langle \hat C \beta,\,\beta\rangle - \langle \hat u,\,\beta\rangle + \lambda_n J(\beta) \tag{13.14}β^​∈β∈Bargmin​21​⟨C^β,β⟩−⟨u^,β⟩+λn​J(β)(13.14)

C^:=1nX∗X=1n∑i=1nxixi∗andu^:=1n∑i=1nyixi=1nX∗y∈Rp.\hat C \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{n} X^* X = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i^* \quad \text{and} \quad \hat u \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n y_i x_i = \frac{1}{n} X^* y \in \mathbb{R}^p.C^:=n1​X∗X=n1​i=1∑n​xi​xi∗​andu^:=n1​i=1∑n​yi​xi​=n1​X∗y∈Rp.

C^→C:=E(xx∗)andu^→u:=E(yx).(13.15)\hat C \rightarrow C \mathrel{:=}\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^*) \quad \text{and} \quad \hat u \rightarrow u \mathrel{:=}\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{y}\mathbf{x}). \tag{13.15}C^→C:=E(xx∗)andu^→u:=E(yx).(13.15)

βˉ∈argminβ  {J(β)  ;  Cβ=u}.\bar \beta\in \underset{\beta}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \left\{ J(\beta) \;;\; C\beta=u \right\} .βˉ​∈βargmin​{J(β);Cβ=u}.

Random design introduces sampling error into the operator as well: C^\hat CC^ estimates CCC. The typical scale is 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​, in the sense that

E(∣ ⁣∣C^−C∣ ⁣∣)=O(n−1/2)andE(∣ ⁣∣u^−u∣ ⁣∣)=O(n−1/2),\mathbb{E}(|\!| \hat C-C |\!|) =O(n^{-1/2}) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbb{E}(|\!| \hat u-u |\!|) =O(n^{-1/2}),E(∣∣C^−C∣∣)=O(n−1/2)andE(∣∣u^−u∣∣)=O(n−1/2),

assuming E(y4)<+∞\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{y}^4)<+\inftyE(y4)<+∞ and E(∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣4)<+∞\mathbb{E}(|\!| \mathbf{x} |\!|^4)<+\inftyE(∣∣x∣∣4)<+∞, which give finite second moments for xx∗\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^*xx∗ and xy\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}xy. Using a linear predictor does not require a correctly specified model y=⟨x, β⟩+w\mathbf{y}=\langle \mathbf{x},\,\beta\rangle + wy=⟨x,β⟩+w with noise www independent of x\mathbf{x}x. The aim is to estimate the best linear predictor βˉ\bar\betaβˉ​.

Extensions of Theorems 9.4, 11.9, and 11.11 can account for covariance-estimation error and yield prediction bounds of the form

E(∣⟨β^, x⟩−⟨βˉ, x⟩∣2)=O(n−κ)\mathbb{E}( |\langle \hat \beta,\,\mathbf{x}\rangle-\langle \bar \beta,\,\mathbf{x}\rangle|^2 ) = O( n^{-\kappa} )E(∣⟨β^​,x⟩−⟨βˉ​,x⟩∣2)=O(n−κ)

E(∣ ⁣∣β^−βˉ∣ ⁣∣2)=O(n−κ′),\mathbb{E}( |\!| \hat \beta-\bar \beta |\!|^2 ) = O( n^{-\kappa'} ),E(∣∣β^​−βˉ​∣∣2)=O(n−κ′),

under suitable source conditions involving CCC and uuu.

Since the noise level is roughly n−12n^{-\frac{1}{2}}n−21​, the ideal cases are when κ=κ′=1\kappa=\kappa'=1κ=κ′=1, which is the so-called linear rate regime.

Support-recovery guarantees can also be derived by extending Theorem 11.15. We now focus on quadratic regularization, a standard regression method. Sparse penalties such as ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 are useful when feature selection or a sparse model is appropriate; their statistical benefit depends on the data and assumptions.

In imaging inverse problems, sparse regularization expresses prior structure of the object being reconstructed.

Ridge regression (quadratic penalization).

For J=∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣2/2J=|\!| \cdot |\!|^2/2J=∣∣⋅∣∣2/2, the estimator (13.14) is obtained in closed form as

β^=(X∗X+nλnIdp)−1X∗y=(C^+λnIdp)−1u^.(13.16)\hat\beta= ( X^* X + n\lambda_n \mathrm{Id}_p )^{-1} X^* y = (\hat C+\lambda_n\mathrm{Id}_p)^{-1}\hat u. \tag{13.16}β^​=(X∗X+nλn​Idp​)−1X∗y=(C^+λn​Idp​)−1u^.(13.16)

β^=X∗(XX∗+nλnIdn)−1y.(13.17)\hat\beta= X^* ( XX^* + n\lambda_n \mathrm{Id}_n )^{-1} y . \tag{13.17}β^​=X∗(XX∗+nλn​Idn​)−1y.(13.17)

The condition λn→0\lambda_n\to0λn​→0 alone is insufficient when small eigenvalues amplify noise. Here is one elementary bound that also applies in a Hilbert feature space.

13.4 Supervised Learning: Classification¶

For classification, the labels are discrete: yi∈Y={1,…,k}y_i \in \mathcal{Y}= \{1,\ldots,k\}yi​∈Y={1,…,k}.

We study two standard methods: nearest neighbors and logistic classification.

Both methods provide useful baselines for assessing more elaborate models.

Nearest-neighbor methods also apply to regression.

13.4.1 Nearest-Neighbor Classification¶

The RRR-nearest-neighbor method (RRR-NN) classifies an input using the labels of its RRR nearest training observations. Increasing RRR reduces sensitivity to individual noisy labels, but excessive smoothing can obscure class boundaries. For consistency, a standard asymptotic choice has R=Rn→∞R=R_n\to\inftyR=Rn​→∞ and Rn/n→0R_n/n\to0Rn​/n→0.

Nearest-neighbor classification is a useful baseline, especially when the feature dimension ppp is small.

The prediction f^(x)∈Y\hat f(x)\in\mathcal{Y}f^​(x)∈Y is the most frequent label among those RRR observations, with a fixed rule for breaking ties. The method is nonparametric: its representation depends on the training sample rather than on a fixed-dimensional parameter vector.

Figure 13.13. Nearest neighbors.

First compute the Euclidean distance from the query xxx to each training observation xix_ixi​.

Sorting the distances generates an indexing σ\sigmaσ (a permutation of {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}{1,…,n}) such that

∣ ⁣∣x−xσ(1)∣ ⁣∣⩽∣ ⁣∣x−xσ(2)∣ ⁣∣⩽…⩽∣ ⁣∣x−xσ(n)∣ ⁣∣.|\!| x-x_{\sigma(1)} |\!| \leqslant|\!| x-x_{\sigma(2)} |\!| \leqslant\ldots \leqslant|\!| x-x_{\sigma(n)} |\!|.∣∣x−xσ(1)​∣∣⩽∣∣x−xσ(2)​∣∣⩽…⩽∣∣x−xσ(n)​∣∣.

For a given RRR, one can compute the “local” histogram of classes around xxx

hℓ(x):=1R#{i∈{1,…,R}:yσ(i)=ℓ}.h_\ell(x)\mathrel{:=}\frac1R\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,R\}:y_{\sigma(i)}=\ell\}.hℓ​(x):=R1​#{i∈{1,…,R}:yσ(i)​=ℓ}.

The predicted class at xxx is an index attaining the largest histogram value:

f^(x)∈argmaxℓ  hℓ(x).\hat f(x) \in \underset{\ell}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}}\; h_\ell(x).f^​(x)∈ℓargmax​hℓ​(x).

Choose RRR by validation or cross-validation. For classification, the validation risk (13.13) typically uses the 0–1 loss, giving the fraction of misclassified observations

Rnˉ:=1nˉ∑j=1nˉδ(yˉj−f^(xˉj))R_{\bar n}\mathrel{:=}\frac1{\bar n}\sum_{j=1}^{\bar n}\delta(\bar y_j-\hat f(\bar x_j))Rnˉ​:=nˉ1​j=1∑nˉ​δ(yˉ​j​−f^​(xˉj​))

where δ(0)=0\delta(0)=0δ(0)=0 and δ(s)=1\delta(s)=1δ(s)=1 if s≠0s \neq 0s=0.

The method also applies to features in a general metric space in place of Rp\mathbb{R}^pRp.

Fast nearest-neighbor search can avoid explicitly sorting every distance.

Increasing RRR leads to smoother class boundaries.

13.4.2 Binary Logistic Classification¶

Logistic classification is a widely used baseline for binary and multiclass prediction. It outputs a probability for each class, providing a richer prediction than a class label alone. The accuracy of these probabilities must still be assessed on held-out data.

The standard name for this model is logistic regression, even when the prediction task is classification.

Support vector machines provide another common approach. Their hinge loss is nonsmooth, and their scores are not probabilities without an additional calibration step. The choice between these methods depends on the task and evaluation criterion.

For the binary formulas below, use labels yi∈Y={−1,1}y_i \in \mathcal{Y}= \{-1,1\}yi​∈Y={−1,1}. In logistic classification, the prediction f(⋅,β)∈[0,1]f(\cdot,\beta) \in [0,1]f(⋅,β)∈[0,1] is a probability for the positive class rather than a class label. We retain the notation fff for this probability predictor.

Approximate risk minimization.

A linear score ⟨x, β⟩\langle x,\,\beta\rangle⟨x,β⟩ defines the classifier sign(⟨x, β⟩)\mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(\langle x,\,\beta\rangle)sign(⟨x,β⟩), with either class assigned when the score is zero. The empirical 0–1 objective counts classification errors, leading to the minimization problem

min⁡β  ∑i=1nℓ0(−yi⟨xi, β⟩)(13.20)\underset{\beta}{\min}\; \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_0(-y_i \langle x_i,\,\beta\rangle) \tag{13.20}βmin​i=1∑n​ℓ0​(−yi​⟨xi​,β⟩)(13.20)

where ℓ0=1[0,+∞)\ell_0=1_{[0,+\infty)}ℓ0​=1[0,+∞)​ counts zero margins as errors. Away from ties, misclassification corresponds to ⟨xi, β⟩\langle x_i,\,\beta\rangle⟨xi​,β⟩ and yiy_iyi​ having different signs, so that in this case ℓ0(−yi⟨xi, β⟩)=1\ell_0(-y_i \langle x_i,\,\beta\rangle)=1ℓ0​(−yi​⟨xi​,β⟩)=1 (and 0 otherwise for correct classification).

The loss ℓ0\ell_0ℓ0​ is nonconvex, and solving (13.20) globally is NP-hard in general. Convex upper bounds on ℓ0\ell_0ℓ0​ provide tractable surrogate objectives.

Two common surrogates are

ℓ(u)=(1+u)+andℓ(u)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(u))/log⁡(2)\ell(u)=(1+u)_+ \quad \text{and} \quad \ell(u)=\log(1+\exp(u))/\log(2)ℓ(u)=(1+u)+​andℓ(u)=log(1+exp(u))/log(2)

These are, respectively, the nonsmooth hinge loss used in support vector machines and the smooth logistic loss. The 1/log⁡(2)1/\log(2)1/log(2) is just a constant which makes ℓ0⩽ℓ\ell_0 \leqslant\ellℓ0​⩽ℓ.

AdaBoost uses the exponential loss ℓ(u)=eu\ell(u)=e^uℓ(u)=eu.

Least squares uses ℓ(u)=(1+u)2\ell(u)=(1+u)^2ℓ(u)=(1+u)2. Its growth for large negative margins makes it a poor pointwise approximation of ℓ0\ell_0ℓ0​, although it can still give useful classifiers.

Unregularized hinge-loss minimization is equivalent to a linear program with nonnegative slack variables:

min⁡u⩾0,β  {∑iui  ;  yi⟨xi, β⟩⩾1−ui for all i}.\underset{u \geqslant 0, \beta}{\min}\; \left\{ \sum_i u_i \;;\; y_i\langle x_i,\,\beta\rangle\geqslant 1-u_i\text{ for all }i \right\} .u⩾0,βmin​{i∑​ui​;yi​⟨xi​,β⟩⩾1−ui​ for all i}.

Logistic loss probabilistic interpretation.

Logistic regression applies a sigmoid to the linear score from Section 13.3.1. The resulting probability predictor is nonlinear. The predicted probability of class +1 is

f(x,β):=θ(⟨x, β⟩)whereθ(s):=es1+es=(1+e−s)−1,(13.21)f(x,\beta) \mathrel{:=}\theta(\langle x,\,\beta\rangle) \quad \text{where} \quad \theta(s) \mathrel{:=}\frac{e^{s}}{1+e^s} = (1+e^{-s})^{-1}, \tag{13.21}f(x,β):=θ(⟨x,β⟩)whereθ(s):=1+eses​=(1+e−s)−1,(13.21)

which is often called the “logit” model.

Despite its simplicity, a linear classifier can be effective when the feature dimension ppp is large.

With s=⟨x, β⟩s=\langle x,\,\beta\rangles=⟨x,β⟩, the predicted probability of class -1 is 1−f(x,β)=θ(−s)1-f(x,\beta)=\theta(-s)1−f(x,β)=θ(−s). The identity θ(−s)=1−θ(s)\theta(-s)=1-\theta(s)θ(−s)=1−θ(s) makes the two probabilities sum to one. It does not require balanced class frequencies; an intercept can account for unequal prior frequencies.

For a nonzero parameter, β/∣ ⁣∣β∣ ⁣∣\beta/|\!| \beta |\!|β/∣∣β∣∣ determines the normal direction of the separating hyperplane, while 1/∣ ⁣∣β∣ ⁣∣1/|\!| \beta |\!|1/∣∣β∣∣ controls the width of the probability transition. For multiclass logistic classification, introduce one weight vector for each of the kkk classes. Collect the vectors β=(βℓ)ℓ=1k\beta= ( \beta_\ell )_{\ell=1}^kβ=(βℓ​)ℓ=1k​ as columns of β∈Rp×k\beta\in \mathbb{R}^{p \times k}β∈Rp×k.

For an input x∈Rpx \in \mathbb{R}^px∈Rp, convert the class scores into probabilities using the softmax model:

f(x,β)=(e⟨x, βℓ⟩∑me⟨x, βm⟩)ℓ(13.24)f(x,\beta) = \left( \frac{ e^{\langle x,\,\beta_\ell\rangle} }{ \sum_m e^{\langle x,\,\beta_m\rangle} } \right)_\ell \tag{13.24}f(x,β)=(∑m​e⟨x,βm​⟩e⟨x,βℓ​⟩​)ℓ​(13.24)

The vector f(x,β)∈[0,1]kf(x,\beta)\in[0,1]^kf(x,β)∈[0,1]k gives the probabilities that xxx belongs to each class, and satisfies ∑ℓf(x,β)ℓ=1\sum_\ell f(x,\beta)_\ell=1∑ℓ​f(x,β)ℓ​=1.

max⁡β∈Rp×k  1n∑i=1nlog⁡(f(xi,β)yi)\underset{\beta\in \mathbb{R}^{p \times k}}{\max}\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \log( f(x_i,\beta)_{y_i} )β∈Rp×kmax​n1​i=1∑n​log(f(xi​,β)yi​​)

Di,ℓ={1ifyi=ℓ,0otherwise.D_{i,\ell} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1 \quad \text{if} \quad y_i=\ell, \\ 0 \text{otherwise}. \end{array} \right.Di,ℓ​={1ifyi​=ℓ,0otherwise.​

and LSE is the log-sum-exp operator

LSE(S)i=log⁡(∑ℓexp⁡(Si,ℓ)),LSE(S)∈Rn.\text{LSE}(S)_i=\log\left(\sum_\ell\exp(S_{i,\ell})\right),\qquad\text{LSE}(S)\in\mathbb{R}^n.LSE(S)i​=log(ℓ∑​exp(Si,ℓ​)),LSE(S)∈Rn.

13.5 Kernel Methods¶

Linear models may fail to capture the geometry needed for a regression or classification task. Moreover, inputs such as strings and graphs need not belong to a vector space.

Kernel methods introduce a feature map into a richer space and apply linear prediction there. This produces nonlinear regression and classification rules while retaining linear-system solvers and convex optimization. The kernel trick expresses the computations through similarities between the nnn observations, without constructing the feature vectors explicitly. Such methods are nonparametric when the number of fitted coefficients grows with nnn, allowing the model to become more expressive as data accumulate.

Algorithms that use the observations xix_ixi​ only through inner products can often be kernelized. Examples include linear regression, nearest-neighbor methods, SVMs, logistic classification, and PCA. We introduce the construction through ridge regression and then extend it to other losses and distance-based methods.

13.5.1 Feature Map and Kernels¶

Let φ:X→H\varphi: \mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{H}φ:X→H be a feature map into a real Hilbert space H\mathcal{H}H, which may be infinite dimensional.

The input space X\mathcal{X}X need not be a vector space. When X=Rp\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^pX=Rp, the choice φ(x)=x\varphi(x)=xφ(x)=x recovers ordinary linear methods.

For regression, we consider predictions which are linear functions over this lifted space, i.e. of the form x↦⟨φ(x), β⟩Hx \mapsto \langle \varphi(x),\,\beta\rangle_\mathcal{H}x↦⟨φ(x),β⟩H​ for some weight vector β∈H\beta\in \mathcal{H}β∈H. For binary classification, one uses x↦sign(⟨φ(x), β⟩H)x \mapsto \mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(\langle \varphi(x),\,\beta\rangle_\mathcal{H})x↦sign(⟨φ(x),β⟩H​).

For scalar inputs (p=1p=1p=1), the feature map φ(x)=(1,x,x2,…,xk)∈Rk+1\varphi(x) = (1,x,x^2,\ldots,x^k)\in\mathbb{R}^{k+1}φ(x)=(1,x,x2,…,xk)∈Rk+1 gives polynomial regression. Multivariate monomials extend this construction to higher-dimensional inputs.

Let Φ=(φ(xi)∗)i=1n\Phi = ( \varphi(x_i)^* )_{i=1}^nΦ=(φ(xi​)∗)i=1n​ be the feature matrix, whose rows are φ(xi)\varphi(x_i)φ(xi​). For H=Rpˉ\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{R}^{\bar p}H=Rpˉ​, it is an ordinary matrix Φ∈Rn×pˉ\Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times \bar p}Φ∈Rn×pˉ​. In an infinite-dimensional feature space, the same notation represents a linear operator.

For λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, consider the regularized empirical-risk problem

If κ\kappaκ is inexpensive to evaluate, forming KKK takes O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) kernel evaluations. A dense direct solve costs O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) operations; an iterative solve costs O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) per matrix-vector product, with the iteration count determined by conditioning and accuracy.

13.5.2 Kernel Design¶

One can also start directly from a kernel κ(x,x′)\kappa(x,x')κ(x,x′) rather than an explicit feature map φ\varphiφ. This is often convenient because kernels can be designed through their geometric properties and combined, for example by addition. The required condition is that every Gram matrix (κ(xi,xj))i,j(\kappa(x_i,x_j))_{i,j}(κ(xi​,xj​))i,j​ be symmetric positive semidefinite. Such kernels are commonly called positive definite kernels; the condition is equivalent to the existence of a Hilbert-space feature map generating the kernel.

The underlying input space need not be Euclidean.

When using the linear kernel κ(x,y)=⟨x, y⟩\kappa(x,y)=\langle x,\,y\rangleκ(x,y)=⟨x,y⟩, one retrieves the linear models studied in the previous section, and the lifting is trivial φ(x)=x\varphi(x)=xφ(x)=x.

A family of popular kernels are polynomial ones, κ(x,x′)=(⟨x, x′⟩+c)a\kappa(x,x') = (\langle x,\,x\prime\rangle+c)^aκ(x,x′)=(⟨x,x′⟩+c)a for a∈N∗a \in \mathbb{N}^*a∈N∗ and c>0c>0c>0, which corresponds to a lifting in finite dimension. For instance, for a=2a=2a=2 and p=2p=2p=2, one has a lifting in dimension 6

κ(x,x′)=(x1x1′+x2x2′+c)2=⟨φ(x), φ(x′)⟩whereφ(x)=(x12,x22,2x1x2,2cx1,2cx2,c)∗∈R6.\kappa(x,x') = \left( x_1x_1'+x_2x_2' + c \right)^2 = \langle \varphi(x),\,\varphi(x')\rangle \quad \text{where} \quad \varphi(x)=(x_1^2,x_2^2,\sqrt{2}x_1x_2,\sqrt{2c}x_1,\sqrt{2c}x_2,c)^* \in \mathbb{R}^6.κ(x,x′)=(x1​x1′​+x2​x2′​+c)2=⟨φ(x),φ(x′)⟩whereφ(x)=(x12​,x22​,2​x1​x2​,2c​x1​,2c​x2​,c)∗∈R6.

A widely used choice on Euclidean spaces is the Gaussian kernel

κ(x,y):=e−∣ ⁣∣x−y∣ ⁣∣22σ2.(13.27)\kappa(x,y) \mathrel{:=}e^{-\frac{|\!| x-y |\!|^2}{2\sigma^2}} . \tag{13.27}κ(x,y):=e−2σ2∣∣x−y∣∣2​.(13.27)

The bandwidth σ>0\sigma>0σ>0 controls the locality of the model and is typically tuned by cross-validation. The Gaussian kernel has the infinite-dimensional feature map φ(x)(t)=(2/(πσ2))p/4exp⁡(−∣ ⁣∣x−t∣ ⁣∣2/σ2)∈L2(Rp)\varphi(x)(t)=(2/(\pi\sigma^2))^{p/4}\exp(-|\!| x-t |\!|^2/\sigma^2)\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^p)φ(x)(t)=(2/(πσ2))p/4exp(−∣∣x−t∣∣2/σ2)∈L2(Rp).

Another related popular kernel is the Laplacian kernel exp⁡(−∣ ⁣∣x−y∣ ⁣∣/σ)\exp(-|\!| x-y |\!|/\sigma)exp(−∣∣x−y∣∣/σ).

More generally, Bochner’s theorem states that a continuous translation-invariant kernel κ(x,x′)=k(x−x′)\kappa(x,x')=k(x-x')κ(x,x′)=k(x−x′) on Rp\mathbb{R}^pRp is positive definite if and only if kkk is the Fourier transform of a finite nonnegative measure. If this measure has an integrable density, a feature map can be built from the square root of that density. When kkk is integrable and its Fourier transform is an integrable function, the condition is k^⩾0\hat k\geqslant 0k^⩾0; strict positivity is not necessary.

Figure 13.20 shows an example of regression using a Gaussian kernel.

Figure 13.20. Regression using a Gaussian kernel.

Kernel on non-Euclidean spaces.

On a general input space X\mathcal{X}X, a real kernel κ\kappaκ must produce a symmetric positive semidefinite Gram matrix K=(κ(xi,xj))i,jK=(\kappa(x_i,x_j))_{i,j}K=(κ(xi​,xj​))i,j​ for every finite collection of inputs. Equivalently, there is a Hilbert space H\mathcal{H}H and a feature map φ:X→H\varphi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{H}φ:X→H such that κ(x,x′)=⟨φ(x), φ(x′)⟩H\kappa(x,x')=\langle \varphi(x),\,\varphi(x')\rangle_\mathcal{H}κ(x,x′)=⟨φ(x),φ(x′)⟩H​.

For instance, if X=P(M)\mathcal{X}= \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M})X=P(M) is the set of measurable sets of finite measure in a measure space (M,μ)(\mathcal{M},\mu)(M,μ), one can define κ(A,B)=μ(A∩B)\kappa(A,B) = \mu(A \cap B)κ(A,B)=μ(A∩B) which corresponds to the lifting φ(A)=1A\varphi(A)=1_Aφ(A)=1A​ so that ⟨φ(A), φ(B)⟩=∫1A(x)1B(x)dμ(x)=μ(A∩B)\langle \varphi(A),\,\varphi(B)\rangle = \int 1_A(x) 1_B(x)\mathrm{d}\mu(x) = \mu(A \cap B)⟨φ(A),φ(B)⟩=∫1A​(x)1B​(x)dμ(x)=μ(A∩B).

Kernels can also be defined on strings and graphs, although their construction is more involved.

When κ(x,x)>0\kappa(x,x)>0κ(x,x)>0 for every input under consideration, the kernel can be normalized to have a unit diagonal. For a translation-invariant kernel on Rp\mathbb{R}^pRp, the diagonal equals the constant k(0)k(0)k(0), so normalization only requires division by k(0)>0k(0)>0k(0)>0. This corresponds to replacing φ(x)\varphi(x)φ(x) by φ(x)/∣ ⁣∣φ(x)∣ ⁣∣H\varphi(x)/|\!| \varphi(x) |\!|_\mathcal{H}φ(x)/∣∣φ(x)∣∣H​ and thus replacing κ(x,x′)\kappa(x,x')κ(x,x′) by κ(x,x′)κ(x,x)κ(x′,x′)\frac{\kappa(x,x')}{\sqrt{\kappa(x,x)}\sqrt{\kappa(x',x')}}κ(x,x)​κ(x′,x′)​κ(x,x′)​.

13.5.3 General Case¶

The least-squares result extends to other losses under the assumptions below. With a squared Hilbert-space norm penalty, the minimizer belongs to a subspace generated by the data, of dimension at most nnn. This representer theorem reduces the problem to finitely many coefficients even when the feature space H\mathcal{H}H is infinite dimensional.

Proposition 13.8

Assume λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 and the losses ℓ(yi,⋅)\ell(y_i,\cdot)ℓ(yi​,⋅) are finite, nonnegative, and convex. The solution β⋆∈H\beta^\star\in\mathcal{H}β⋆∈H of

min⁡β∈H  ∑i=1nℓ(yi,⟨φ(xi), β⟩)+λ2∣ ⁣∣β∣ ⁣∣H2=L(Φβ,y)+λ2∣ ⁣∣β∣ ⁣∣H2(13.28)\underset{\beta\in \mathcal{H}}{\min}\; \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(y_i, \langle \varphi(x_i),\,\beta\rangle) + \frac{\lambda}{2} |\!| \beta |\!|_\mathcal{H}^2 = \mathcal{L}(\Phi \beta,y) + \frac{\lambda}{2} |\!| \beta |\!|_\mathcal{H}^2 \tag{13.28}β∈Hmin​i=1∑n​ℓ(yi​,⟨φ(xi​),β⟩)+2λ​∣∣β∣∣H2​=L(Φβ,y)+2λ​∣∣β∣∣H2​(13.28)

is unique and can be written as

β=Φ∗c⋆=∑ici⋆φ(xi)∈H(13.29)\beta= \Phi^* c^\star = \sum_i c_i^\star \varphi(x_i) \in \mathcal{H} \tag{13.29}β=Φ∗c⋆=i∑​ci⋆​φ(xi​)∈H(13.29)

where c⋆∈Rnc^\star\in\mathbb{R}^nc⋆∈Rn is a solution of

min⁡c∈Rn  L(Kc,y)+λ2⟨Kc, c⟩Rn(13.30)\underset{c \in \mathbb{R}^n}{\min}\; \mathcal{L}(K c,y) + \frac{\lambda}{2} \langle K c,\,c\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^n} \tag{13.30}c∈Rnmin​L(Kc,y)+2λ​⟨Kc,c⟩Rn​(13.30)

where we defined

K:=ΦΦ∗=(⟨φ(xi), φ(xj)⟩H)i,j=1n∈Rn×n.K\mathrel{:=}\Phi\Phi^* = ( \langle \varphi(x_i),\,\varphi(x_j)\rangle_\mathcal{H})_{i,j=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}.K:=ΦΦ∗=(⟨φ(xi​),φ(xj​)⟩H​)i,j=1n​∈Rn×n.
Proof

Let V=Span{φ(xi):1⩽i⩽n}V=\mathop{\mathrm{Span}}\{\varphi(x_i):1\leqslant i\leqslant n\}V=Span{φ(xi​):1⩽i⩽n} and decompose β=βV+β⊥\beta=\beta_V+\beta_\perpβ=βV​+β⊥​ orthogonally. Predictions on the data depend only on βV\beta_VβV​, while ∣ ⁣∣β∣ ⁣∣2=∣ ⁣∣βV∣ ⁣∣2+∣ ⁣∣β⊥∣ ⁣∣2|\!| \beta |\!|^2=|\!| \beta_V |\!|^2+|\!| \beta_\perp |\!|^2∣∣β∣∣2=∣∣βV​∣∣2+∣∣β⊥​∣∣2. Since λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, a minimizer has β⊥=0\beta_\perp=0β⊥​=0. The restriction to the finite-dimensional space VVV is continuous, coercive, and strictly convex, hence has a unique minimizer. Substituting β=Φ∗c\beta=\Phi^*cβ=Φ∗c gives (13.30); the coefficient vector ccc need not be unique if KKK is singular.

Equation (13.29) places the minimizer in a subspace of dimension at most nnn, spanned by the observed feature vectors φ(xi)\varphi(x_i)φ(xi​).

The potentially infinite-dimensional problem (13.28) becomes the finite-dimensional problem (13.30). A dense first-order iteration costs O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) once the kernel matrix is available. A low-rank approximation K≈Φ~∗Φ~K \approx \tilde\Phi^* \tilde \PhiK≈Φ~∗Φ~ can reduce this cost further by introducing a smaller approximate feature space.

For classification applications, one can use for ℓ\ellℓ a hinge or a logistic loss function, and then the decision boundary is computed following (13.26) using kernel evaluations only as

sign(⟨β⋆, φ(x)⟩H)=sign(∑ici⋆κ(x,xi)).\mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(\langle \beta^\star,\,\varphi(x)\rangle_\mathcal{H}) = \mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(\sum_i c_i^\star \kappa(x,x_i)).sign(⟨β⋆,φ(x)⟩H​)=sign(i∑​ci⋆​κ(x,xi​)).

Figure 13.21 illustrates a nonlinear decision boundary in two dimensions. The decision rule is linear in the feature space H\mathcal{H}H; evaluating it through the nonlinear feature map produces a curved boundary in the input space.

Nearest-neighbor classification (Section 13.4.1) and regression can likewise use distances in feature space, computed entirely from the kernel:

∣ ⁣∣φ(xi)−φ(xj)∣ ⁣∣H2=κ(xi,xi)+κ(xj,xj)−2κ(xi,xj).|\!| \varphi(x_i)-\varphi(x_j) |\!|_\mathcal{H}^2 = \kappa(x_i,x_i)+\kappa(x_j,x_j) - 2 \kappa(x_i,x_j).∣∣φ(xi​)−φ(xj​)∣∣H2​=κ(xi​,xi​)+κ(xj​,xj​)−2κ(xi​,xj​).

13.6 Probably Approximately Correct Learning¶

This section introduces Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, which studies generalization guarantees under explicit complexity and sampling assumptions. Distribution-free bounds avoid further restrictions on the data distribution. The main reference (and in particular the proofs of the mentioned results) for this section is the book “Foundations of Machine Learning” by Mehryar Mohri, Afshin Rostamizadeh, and Ameet Talwalkar https://cs.nyu.edu/~mohri/mlbook/.

Assume the observations D:=(xi,yi)i=1n\mathcal{D}\mathrel{:=}(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^nD:=(xi​,yi​)i=1n​ are independent and identically distributed copies of a random pair (X,Y)(X,Y)(X,Y) taking values in X×Y\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}X×Y. From this sample, we seek a predictor f:X→Yf : \mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{Y}f:X→Y with risk close to the smallest achievable value:

L(f):=E(ℓ(Y,f(X)))=∫X×Yℓ(y,f(x))dPX,Y(x,y)L(f) \mathrel{:=}\mathbb{E}( \ell(Y,f(X)) ) = \int_{\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}} \ell(y,f(x)) \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{X,Y}(x,y)L(f):=E(ℓ(Y,f(X)))=∫X×Y​ℓ(y,f(x))dPX,Y​(x,y)

where ℓ:Y×Y→R\ell : \mathcal{Y}\times \mathcal{Y}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}ℓ:Y×Y→R is some loss function.

To estimate this minimizer, we select a class of functions F\mathcal{F}F and minimize the empirical risk

f^∈argminf∈F  L^(f):=1n∑i=1nℓ(yi,f(xi)).\hat f \in \underset{f \in \mathcal{F}}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \hat L(f) \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(y_i,f(x_i)).f^​∈f∈Fargmin​L^(f):=n1​i=1∑n​ℓ(yi​,f(xi​)).

We assume a measurable minimizer exists. It is random because it depends on the sample D\mathcal{D}D.

Example 13.9 (Regression and classification)

In regression, Y=R\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}Y=R and the most common choice of loss is ℓ(y,z)=(y−z)2\ell(y,z) = (y-z)^2ℓ(y,z)=(y−z)2. For binary classification, Y={−1,+1}\mathcal{Y}=\{-1,+1\}Y={−1,+1} and the ideal choice is the 0-1 loss ℓ(y,z)=1y≠z\ell(y,z)=1_{y \neq z}ℓ(y,z)=1y=z​.

For many useful classes F\mathcal{F}F, minimizing the empirical 0–1 risk is computationally difficult. A common alternative uses a surrogate loss of the form ℓ(y,z)=Γ(−yz)\ell(y,z) = \Gamma(-yz)ℓ(y,z)=Γ(−yz) where Γ\GammaΓ is a convex function upper-bounding 1R+1_{\mathbb{R}^+}1R+​, which makes empirical risk minimization convex when the real-valued score class is convex.

PAC learning seeks a bound on the excess risk L(f^)−inf⁡(L)⩾0L(\hat f)-\inf(L)\geqslant 0L(f^​)−inf(L)⩾0 that holds with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta1−δ. The bound depends on the sample size nnn and confidence parameter δ\deltaδ. For the excess risk to vanish, the approximation class must become sufficiently rich while its statistical complexity remains controlled. Quantitative approximation rates require distributional assumptions, although some consistency results hold without them.

13.6.1 Nonparametric Models and Calibration¶

If F\mathcal{F}F contains all measurable functions, a minimizer f⋆f^\starf⋆ of LLL is called a Bayes estimator: it achieves the smallest possible population risk.

Risk decomposition

Denoting

α(z∣x):=EY(ℓ(Y,z)∣X=x)=∫Yℓ(y,z)dPY∣X(y∣x)\alpha(z|x) \mathrel{:=}\mathbb{E}_Y(\ell(Y,z)|X=x) = \int_\mathcal{Y}\ell(y,z)\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{Y|X}(y|x)α(z∣x):=EY​(ℓ(Y,z)∣X=x)=∫Y​ℓ(y,z)dPY∣X​(y∣x)

the average loss of predicting z∈Yz\in\mathcal{Y}z∈Y at input x∈Xx\in\mathcal{X}x∈X, the risk decomposes as

L(f)=∫X[∫Yℓ(y,f(x))dPY∣X(y∣x)]dPX(x)=∫Xα(f(x)∣x)dPX(x)L(f) = \int_\mathcal{X}\left[ \int_\mathcal{Y}\ell(y,f(x)) \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{Y|X}(y|x) \right] \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_X(x) = \int_\mathcal{X}\alpha(f(x)|x) \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_X(x)L(f)=∫X​[∫Y​ℓ(y,f(x))dPY∣X​(y∣x)]dPX​(x)=∫X​α(f(x)∣x)dPX​(x)

Consequently, f⋆f^\starf⋆ can be chosen separately at each input xxx by solving

f⋆(x)=argminz  α(z∣x).f^\star(x) = \underset{z}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \alpha(z|x).f⋆(x)=zargmin​α(z∣x).
Example 13.10 (Regression)

For squared-loss regression with E(Y2)<∞\mathbb{E}(Y^2)<\inftyE(Y2)<∞, one has f⋆(x)=E(Y∣X=x)=∫YydPY∣X(y∣x)f^\star(x)=\mathbb{E}(Y|X=x) = \int_\mathcal{Y}y \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{Y|X}(y|x)f⋆(x)=E(Y∣X=x)=∫Y​ydPY∣X​(y∣x), which is the conditional expectation.

Example 13.11 (Classification)

For classification applications, where Y={−1,1}\mathcal{Y}= \{-1,1\}Y={−1,1}, it is convenient to introduce η(x):=PY∣X(y=1∣x)∈[0,1]\eta(x) \mathrel{:=}\mathbb{P}_{Y|X}(y=1|x) \in [0,1]η(x):=PY∣X​(y=1∣x)∈[0,1].

If the two classes are separable, then η(x)∈{0,1}\eta(x) \in \{0,1\}η(x)∈{0,1} for PX\mathbb{P}_XPX​-almost every xxx.

For the 0-1 loss ℓ(y,z)=1y≠z=1(0,+∞)(−yz)\ell(y,z)=1_{y\neq z}=1_{(0,+\infty)}(-yz)ℓ(y,z)=1y=z​=1(0,+∞)​(−yz), one may choose f⋆=sign(2η−1)f^\star=\mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(2\eta-1)f⋆=sign(2η−1), with either class selected at a tie and L(f⋆)=EX(min⁡(η(X),1−η(X)))L(f^\star) = \mathbb{E}_X( \min(\eta(X),1-\eta(X)) )L(f⋆)=EX​(min(η(X),1−η(X))).

The conditional probability η\etaη is unknown and must be estimated from D\mathcal{D}D. Direct 0–1 optimization is computationally difficult for many useful classes F\mathcal{F}F.

For a margin loss ℓ(y,z)=Γ(−yz)\ell(y,z)=\Gamma(-yz)ℓ(y,z)=Γ(−yz), an unconstrained Bayes score satisfies

f⋆(x)=argminz  (α(z∣x)=η(x)Γ(−z)+(1−η(x))Γ(z)),f^\star(x) = \underset{z}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \Big( \alpha(z|x) = \eta(x) \Gamma(-z) + (1-\eta(x)) \Gamma(z) \Big),f⋆(x)=zargmin​(α(z∣x)=η(x)Γ(−z)+(1−η(x))Γ(z)),

Thus the optimal score is a function of η(x)\eta(x)η(x). This argmin notation presumes attainment; for logistic loss and η∈{0,1}\eta\in\{0,1\}η∈{0,1}, the infimum is approached only as the score tends to the appropriate infinity.

Calibration in the classification setup

We would like the classifier sign(f⋆)\mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(f^\star)sign(f⋆) to agree with a Bayes classifier for the 0–1 loss, namely sign(2η−1)\mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(2\eta-1)sign(2η−1) away from ties. This property is called classification calibration. It does not require the scores f⋆f^\starf⋆ and 2η−12\eta-12η−1 themselves to agree. The following result characterizes calibration for finite convex margin losses.

Proposition 13.12

A loss ℓ\ellℓ associated to a finite, nonnegative convex Γ\GammaΓ is calibrated if and only if Γ\GammaΓ is differentiable at 0 and Γ′(0)>0\Gamma'(0)>0Γ′(0)>0.

Both hinge and logistic loss satisfy this calibration criterion.

Let LΓL_\GammaLΓ​ be the risk for ℓ(y,z)=Γ(−yz)\ell(y,z)=\Gamma(-yz)ℓ(y,z)=Γ(−yz) and let L0–1L_{0\text{--}1}L0–1​ be classification risk, with a fixed tie-breaking convention. Quantitative calibration bounds have the form

0⩽L0–1(signf)−inf⁡L0–1⩽Ψ(LΓ(f)−inf⁡LΓ)(13.31)0 \leqslant L_{0\text{--}1}(\mathop{\mathrm{sign}}f)-\inf L_{0\text{--}1} \leqslant\Psi( L_{\Gamma}(f) - \inf L_{\Gamma} ) \tag{13.31}0⩽L0–1​(signf)−infL0–1​⩽Ψ(LΓ​(f)−infLΓ​)(13.31)

for some increasing function Ψ:R+→R+\Psi : \mathbb{R}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+Ψ:R+→R+ satisfying Ψ(0)=0\Psi(0)=0Ψ(0)=0. Such a control ensures in particular that if f⋆f^\starf⋆ minimizes LΓL_{\Gamma}LΓ​, its induced classifier has Bayes-optimal 0–1 risk. At η=1/2\eta=1/2η=1/2, either class is optimal; away from ties, its sign agrees almost surely with that of 2η−12\eta-12η−1.

For hinge loss, the calibration bound holds with Ψ(r)=r\Psi(r)=rΨ(r)=r. For logistic loss, it holds with Ψ(s)=2s\Psi(s)=\sqrt{2s}Ψ(s)=2s​.

13.6.2 PAC bounds¶

Approximation–estimation decomposition.

For a class F\mathcal{F}F of functions, the excess risk of the empirical estimator

f^∈argminf∈F  L^(f)\hat f \in \underset{f \in \mathcal{F}}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \hat L(f)f^​∈f∈Fargmin​L^(f)

decomposes into a random estimation error and a deterministic approximation error:

L(f^)−inf⁡L=[L(f^)−inf⁡FL]+A(F)whereA(F):=[inf⁡FL−inf⁡L].(13.32)L(\hat f) - \inf L = \Big[ L(\hat f) - \inf_{\mathcal{F}} L \Big] + \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{F}) \quad \text{where} \quad \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{F}) \mathrel{:=}\Big[ \inf_{\mathcal{F}} L - \inf L \Big]. \tag{13.32}L(f^​)−infL=[L(f^​)−Finf​L]+A(F)whereA(F):=[Finf​L−infL].(13.32)

This separates the effects of sampling and model approximation.

Enlarging a nested class F\mathcal{F}F reduces approximation error but typically increases the estimation-error bound. Choose the class size as a function of nnn to balance these effects and avoid overfitting.

Approximation error.

A quantitative approximation bound requires assumptions on f⋆f^\starf⋆. No-free-lunch results rule out a uniform distribution-free approximation rate over all measurable targets.

The following example illustrates such a bound.

Example 13.13 (Linearly parameterized functionals)

A popular class of functions consists of linearly parameterized maps of the form

f(x)=fw(x)=⟨φ(x), w⟩Hf(x) = f_w(x) = \langle \varphi(x),\,w\rangle_\mathcal{H}f(x)=fw​(x)=⟨φ(x),w⟩H​

where φ:X→H\varphi: \mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{H}φ:X→H maps inputs to a Hilbert feature space. For X=Rp\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^pX=Rp, the identity map φ(x)=x\varphi(x)=xφ(x)=x recovers ordinary linear models. One can also consider for instance polynomial features, φ(x)=(1,x1,…,xp,x12,x1x2,…)\varphi(x)=(1, x_1,\ldots,x_p,x_1^2,x_1 x_2, \ldots)φ(x)=(1,x1​,…,xp​,x12​,x1​x2​,…), giving rise to polynomial regression and polynomial classification boundaries.

with associated kernel k(x,x′):=⟨φ(x), φ(x′)⟩Hk(x,x') \mathrel{:=}\langle \varphi(x),\,\varphi(x')\rangle_\mathcal{H}k(x,x′):=⟨φ(x),φ(x′)⟩H​. We use the feature-map representation directly below.

Estimation error.

Concentration inequalities control sampling fluctuations, while a bound on the complexity of F\mathcal{F}F makes this control uniform over the model class.

The estimation error is controlled by uniform deviations between LLL and L^\hat LL^. Let g∈Fg\in\mathcal{F}g∈F attain inf⁡FL\inf_{\mathcal{F}}LinfF​L, assuming for simplicity that such a minimizer exists. Then

L(f^)−inf⁡FL=[L(f^)−L^(f^)]+[L^(f^)−L^(g)]+[L^(g)−L(g)]⩽2sup⁡f∈F∣L^(f)−L(f)∣(13.33)L(\hat f) - \inf_{\mathcal{F}} L = \Big[L(\hat f) - \hat L(\hat f)\Big] + \Big[\hat L(\hat f) - \hat L(g)\Big] + \Big[\hat L(g)-L(g)\Big] \leqslant 2 \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}}|\hat L(f) - L(f)| \tag{13.33}L(f^​)−Finf​L=[L(f^​)−L^(f^​)]+[L^(f^​)−L^(g)]+[L^(g)−L(g)]⩽2f∈Fsup​∣L^(f)−L(f)∣(13.33)

since L^(f^)−L^(g)⩽0\hat L(\hat f) - \hat L(g) \leqslant 0L^(f^​)−L^(g)⩽0.

Define the two one-sided deviations

Δ+(D)=sup⁡f∈F(L(f)−L^(f)),Δ−(D)=sup⁡f∈F(L^(f)−L(f)).\Delta_+(\mathcal{D})=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}(L(f)-\hat L(f)),\qquad \Delta_-(\mathcal{D})=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}(\hat L(f)-L(f)).Δ+​(D)=f∈Fsup​(L(f)−L^(f)),Δ−​(D)=f∈Fsup​(L^(f)−L(f)).

In the case where F={⟨φ(⋅), w⟩H  ;  ∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣⩽R}\mathcal{F}= \left\{ \langle \varphi(\cdot),\,w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \;;\; |\!| w |\!| \leqslant R \right\}F={⟨φ(⋅),w⟩H​;∣∣w∣∣⩽R} where ∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣|\!| \cdot |\!|∣∣⋅∣∣ is some norm on H\mathcal{H}H, one has

Rn(F)⩽RE(∣ ⁣∣φ(X)∣ ⁣∣H2)n.\mathcal{R}_n(\mathcal{F}) \leqslant\frac{R \sqrt{\mathbb{E}(|\!| \varphi(X) |\!|_\mathcal{H}^2)} }{\sqrt{n}}.Rn​(F)⩽n​RE(∣∣φ(X)∣∣H2​)​​.

The bound has no explicit dependence on feature dimension and also applies to infinite-dimensional RKHS feature maps with finite second moment.

For fixed RRR and fixed loss constants, the estimation bound in (13.35) decays as 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​; the approximation error remains a separate term.

The radius RRR controls the balance between approximation and estimation. In practice, it can be selected by cross-validation.

Example 13.19 (Application to SVM classification)

The 0–1 loss is not Lipschitz in a real-valued score. For a margin ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0, use the bounded ramp loss

Γρ(s)=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,1+s/ρ}}.\Gamma_\rho(s)=\min\{1,\max\{0,1+s/\rho\}\}.Γρ​(s)=min{1,max{0,1+s/ρ}}.

1[0,+∞)(s)⩽Γρ(s)⩽max⁡{1+s/ρ,0}.1_{[0,+\infty)}(s)\leqslant\Gamma_\rho(s)\leqslant\max\{1+s/\rho,0\}.1[0,+∞)​(s)⩽Γρ​(s)⩽max{1+s/ρ,0}.

The left inequality counts score ties as errors, so it also bounds the risk of any fixed tie-breaking classifier. For FR={fw:∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣H⩽R}\mathcal{F}_R=\{f_w:|\!| w |\!|_\mathcal{H}\leqslant R\}FR​={fw​:∣∣w∣∣H​⩽R}, the one-sided concentration and symmetrization bounds imply, simultaneously for every f∈FRf\in\mathcal{F}_Rf∈FR​, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta1−δ,

L0–1(signf)⩽1n∑imax⁡{1−yif(xi)/ρ,0}+2RρE∣ ⁣∣φ(X)∣ ⁣∣H2n+log⁡(1/δ)2n.L_{0\text{--}1}(\mathop{\mathrm{sign}}f)\leqslant \frac1n\sum_i\max\{1-y_if(x_i)/\rho,0\} +\frac{2R}{\rho}\sqrt{\frac{\mathbb{E}|\!| \varphi(X) |\!|_\mathcal{H}^2}{n}} +\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2n}}.L0–1​(signf)⩽n1​i∑​max{1−yi​f(xi​)/ρ,0}+ρ2R​nE∣∣φ(X)∣∣H2​​​+2nlog(1/δ)​​.

This bound applies to a data-dependent predictor, including an empirical hinge-loss minimizer in the ball. It does not require minimizing the nonconvex ramp loss. In practice, the norm constraint is often replaced by a penalty:

min⁡w  1n∑imax⁡{1−yifw(xi),0}+λ∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣H2,λ>0.(13.36)\underset{w}{\min}\;\frac1n\sum_i\max\{1-y_if_w(x_i),0\}+\lambda|\!| w |\!|_\mathcal{H}^2,\qquad\lambda>0. \tag{13.36}wmin​n1​i∑​max{1−yi​fw​(xi​),0}+λ∣∣w∣∣H2​,λ>0.(13.36)

This is the kernel support vector machine.

Remark 13.20 (Resolution using the kernel trick)

The kernel trick reduces problems such as (13.36), of the form

min⁡w∈H  1n∑i=1nℓ(yi,⟨w, φ(xi)⟩)+λ∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣H2(13.37)\underset{w \in \mathcal{H}}{\min}\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(y_i, \langle w,\,\varphi(x_i)\rangle ) + \lambda |\!| w |\!|_\mathcal{H}^2 \tag{13.37}w∈Hmin​n1​i=1∑n​ℓ(yi​,⟨w,φ(xi​)⟩)+λ∣∣w∣∣H2​(13.37)

to optimization over nnn coefficients, even when the feature space is infinite dimensional. The representer theorem gives w⋆=∑i=1nci⋆φ(xi)w^\star = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i^\star \varphi(x_i)w⋆=∑i=1n​ci⋆​φ(xi​) for some c⋆∈Rnc^\star \in \mathbb{R}^nc⋆∈Rn: an orthogonal component would leave the predictions unchanged and strictly increase the positive norm penalty.

Substituting this representation into (13.37) reduces the data dependence to the empirical kernel matrix K=(k(xi,xj):=⟨φ(xi), φ(xj)⟩)i,j=1n∈Rn×nK = ( k(x_i,x_j)\mathrel{:=}\langle \varphi(x_i),\,\varphi(x_j)\rangle )_{i,j=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}K=(k(xi​,xj​):=⟨φ(xi​),φ(xj​)⟩)i,j=1n​∈Rn×n since it reads

min⁡c∈Rn  1n∑i=1nℓ(yi,(Kc)i)+λ⟨Kc, c⟩\underset{c \in \mathbb{R}^n}{\min}\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(y_i, (K c)_i) + \lambda \langle K c,\,c\ranglec∈Rnmin​n1​i=1∑n​ℓ(yi​,(Kc)i​)+λ⟨Kc,c⟩

From any optimal c⋆c^\starc⋆ of this convex program (which need not be strictly convex when KKK is singular), the estimator is evaluated as fw⋆(x)=⟨w⋆, φ(x)⟩=∑ici⋆k(xi,x)f_{w^\star}(x)=\langle w^\star,\,\varphi(x)\rangle = \sum_i c_i^\star k(x_i,x)fw⋆​(x)=⟨w⋆,φ(x)⟩=∑i​ci⋆​k(xi​,x).
